steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on bounded-suboptimal Conflict-Based Search for multi-agent path finding, where we show that a weighted cost-to-go heuristic can be used together with the conflict heuristic in the low-level planner. Cover the background on MAPF, Prioritized Planning and the CBS variants, and end with our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What MAPF is and why it matters
  - collision-free paths for team of agents, known environment, minimize travel times measure
  - applications: automated warehouses, robot soccer, collaborative manufacturing, coverage, others (cite each)
  - NP-complete (cite)
- Prioritized Planning (PP)
  - fast; plans agents sequentially, avoiding earlier agents with better "priority" (cite)
  - applied to several domains (cite)
  - no guarantees on completeness or bounded suboptimality
- CBS
  - popular, complete and optimal; low-level single agent planner + high-level constraint tree (CT) resolving conflicts
  - speedups by reducing CT size: pruning branches, selectively expanding branches, sets of constraints, symmetries, better high-level heuristics (cite)
- Suboptimal CBS variants
  - ECBS (cite): first bounded-suboptimal CBS; focal search high level + focal search low level minimizing path conflicts -> smaller CT
  - ECBS: weighted cost-to-go in low level -> many conflicts, larger CT, [quote: ECBS's "ineffective" remark]; motivation for reducing conflicts instead
  - EECBS (cite): Explicit Estimation Search (cite) on high level, same low level focal search
  - CCBS (cite): SIPP (cite) to speed up low level by reasoning about waits; no weighted heuristic
  - no prior work effectively used weighted cost-to-go in CBS; norm: more conflicts, worse performance, or loses bounded sub-optimality
- Our insight and contributions
  - use weighted cost-to-go together with conflict heuristic
  - first bounded sub-optimal CBS methods doing this in single agent planner
  - performance controlled by relative weight of cost-to-go vs conflict heuristic; trade off low-level vs high-level work (Figure 1)
  - counter to single agent planning experience (expect weighted heuristic to speed up path finding)
  - contributions: (1) weighted cost-to-go in open queue + path lower bounds vs CBS improvements; (2) combine with weighted conflict heuristic ratio in focal queue, relative weight dictates performance, analysis vs CBS and single-agent intuition; (3) PP as a particular step of suboptimal CBS, our methods the natural generalization

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is the problem where we need to compute paths for a team of agents in a known environment so that they do not collide, and we want to minimize some measure of their travel times. Many real-world tasks need this, for example running automated warehouses smoothly, robot soccer, collaborative manufacturing, coverage, and other ones. MAPF is a hard problem, and it has been shown to be NP-complete.

Prioritized Planning (PP) is one approach to multi-agent planning that is fast. It plans the agents one after another, and each agent avoids the earlier agents that have a better "priority". It has been applied in several domains. But PP does not give any guarantees on completeness or on bounded suboptimality.

Conflict-Based Search (CBS) is a popular MAPF solver which is complete and optimal. It uses a single agent planner on the low level and a constraint tree (CT) on the high level to resolve conflicts. There are several methods that make CBS faster by making the CT smaller, by explicitly pruning branches, by selectively expanding branches, by adding sets of constraints, by detecting symmetries, and by improving the high-level heuristics.

- Suboptimal CBS variants
  - ECBS (cite): first bounded-suboptimal CBS; focal search on high level + focal search on low level minimizing path conflicts -> smaller CT
  - ECBS says weighted cost-to-go in low level gives many conflicts, larger CT, "ineffective in [their] experiments"; their motivation for reducing conflicts instead
  - EECBS (cite): Explicit Estimation Search (cite) on high level, same low level focal search
  - CCBS (cite): SIPP (cite) to speed up low level by reasoning about waits; no weighted heuristic
  - no prior work effectively used weighted cost-to-go in CBS; norm: more conflicts, worse performance, or loses bounded sub-optimality
- Our insight and contributions
  - weighted cost-to-go together with conflict heuristic; first bounded sub-optimal CBS methods doing this in the single agent planner
  - performance controlled by relative weight of the two heuristics; trade off low-level vs high-level work (Figure 1)
  - counter to single agent planning experience
  - contributions: (1) weighted cost-to-go in open queue, path lower bounds vs CBS improvements; (2) weighted conflict heuristic ratio in focal queue, relative weight dictates performance, extra analysis; (3) PP as a particular step of suboptimal CBS, our methods generalize it

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is the problem where we need to compute paths for a team of agents in a known environment so that they do not collide, and we want to minimize some measure of their travel times. Many real-world tasks need this, for example running automated warehouses smoothly, robot soccer, collaborative manufacturing, coverage, and other ones. MAPF is a hard problem, and it has been shown to be NP-complete.

Prioritized Planning (PP) is one approach to multi-agent planning that is fast. It plans the agents one after another, and each agent avoids the earlier agents that have a better "priority". It has been applied in several domains. But PP does not give any guarantees on completeness or on bounded suboptimality.

Conflict-Based Search (CBS) is a popular MAPF solver which is complete and optimal. It uses a single agent planner on the low level and a constraint tree (CT) on the high level to resolve conflicts. There are several methods that make CBS faster by making the CT smaller, by explicitly pruning branches, by selectively expanding branches, by adding sets of constraints, by detecting symmetries, and by improving the high-level heuristics.

Enhanced CBS (ECBS) was the first bounded-suboptimal version of CBS. It uses focal search on the high level, and it also uses another focal search planner on the low level which minimizes the path conflicts with other agents, so the CT size goes down. ECBS specifically mentions that when the low level planner is changed to use a weighted cost-to-go heuristic it returns paths with many conflicts, which leads to a larger CT tree, and that this proved "ineffective in [their] experiments", and they use this as direct motivation for reducing the path conflicts instead. Explicit Estimation CBS (EECBS) replaces the high level focal search of ECBS with Explicit Estimation Search, but it keeps the same focal search on the low level. Continuous-time CBS (CCBS) uses Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) to make the low level search faster by reasoning about waits, but it also does not use a weighted heuristic. As far as we know, no prior work has used a weighted cost-to-go heuristic effectively in any way in the CBS framework, and the usual belief is that doing this would lead to more conflicts, make performance worse, or remove bounded sub-optimality.

Our first insight is that the weighted cost-to-go heuristic can be used together with the conflict heuristic. We introduce the first bounded sub-optimal CBS methods that put a weighted cost-to-go heuristic together with the conflict heuristic in the single agent planner of CBS. We find that the performance (and large performance gains) is controlled by the relative weight between the cost-to-go heuristic and the conflict heuristic, and this lets us trade off work on the low level and work on the high level, see Figure 1. This is the opposite of what researchers familiar with single agent planning would expect, since there the weighted cost-to-go heuristic should improve performance by finding paths faster. Our contributions are:

- 1. Using the weighted cost-to-go heuristic in the open queue, and studying how the lower bounds of the paths interact with some CBS improvements.

- 2. Combining the weighted cost-to-go heuristic with a weighted conflict heuristic ratio in the focal queue, and showing that the relative weight, and not the weighted heuristic, is what dictates performance. We also give more analysis and show that this behaviour is new compared to the existing intuition for CBS and for single-agent planning.

- 3. Reducing PP to a particular step of suboptimal CBS, and showing that our methods are the natural generalization of it.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is the problem of computing collision-free paths for a team of agents in a known environment while minimizing some measure of their travel times. This is required for several real-world tasks such as the smooth operation of automated warehouses [1], robot soccer [2], collaborative manufacturing [3], coverage [4], and others. MAPF is a challenging problem and has been shown to be NP-complete [5].

Prioritized Planning (PP) [6] is a fast multi-agent planning approach that plans agents sequentially, avoiding earlier agents with better "priority", and it has been applied to several domains [7,8,9]. However, PP provides no guarantees on completeness or bounded suboptimality.

Conflict-Based Search (CBS) is a popular complete and optimal MAPF solver that uses a low-level single agent planner and a high-level constraint tree (CT) to resolve conflicts. Several methods speed up CBS by reducing the size of the CT, by explicitly pruning branches, selectively expanding branches, adding sets of constraints, detecting symmetries, and improving high-level heuristics [10,11,12,13,14].

Enhanced CBS (ECBS) [15] introduced the first bounded-suboptimal version of CBS, using a focal search on the high level as well as another focal search planner on the low level that minimizes path conflicts with other agents and thereby decreases the CT size. ECBS specifically mentions that modifying the low level planner to use a weighted cost-to-go heuristic returns paths with many conflicts, leading to a larger CT tree, and that this proved "ineffective in [their] experiments", as direct motivation for reducing path conflicts instead. Explicit Estimation CBS (EECBS) [16] replaces ECBS's high level focal search with Explicit Estimation Search [17] but keeps the same low level focal search. Continuous-time CBS (CCBS) [18] incorporates Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) [19] to speed up the low level search by reasoning about waits, but it also does not use a weighted heuristic. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has effectively used a weighted cost-to-go heuristic in any manner in the CBS framework, and the prevailing norm is that doing so would lead to more conflicts, reduce performance, or remove bounded sub-optimality.

Our initial insight is that we can use the weighted cost-to-go heuristic along with the conflict heuristic. We introduce the first bounded sub-optimal CBS methods that incorporate a weighted cost-to-go heuristic together with the conflict heuristic within CBS's single agent planner. We find that performance (and large performance gains) is controlled by the relative weight of the cost-to-go and conflict heuristic, which lets us trade off low-level and high-level work, see Figure 1. This runs counter to the experience of researchers familiar with single agent planning, where we would expect the weighted cost-to-go heuristic to improve performance by finding paths faster. Our contributions are:

- 1. Incorporating the weighted cost-to-go heuristic in the open queue, and studying how the path lower bounds interact with certain CBS improvements.

- 2. Combining the weighted cost-to-go heuristic with a weighted conflict heuristic ratio in the focal queue and demonstrating that the relative weight, not the weighted heuristic, dictates performance. We provide additional analysis and show how this behaviour is novel with respect to existing CBS and single-agent planning intuition.

- 3. Reducing PP to a particular step of suboptimal CBS and showing that our methods are its natural generalization.
